7.title: The quiz-score problem
body: A school records five quiz scores, each from 0 to 20.
Input: five valid scores. Process: total, mean and highest.
Output: the mean and highest score. Store results if they must survive closing the program.
7.check: Which details could you abstract away?
7.answer: The colour of the classroom walls is irrelevant; the number of scores and valid range are essential.
7.teacher: Starter: ask pairs to write the input, process, output and storage requirements before showing the model.

7.title: Inputs, processes, outputs and storage
body: Five scores must lie between 0 and 20.
Saving the result is a separate requirement from displaying it.
7.check: Which part checks that 24 is unacceptable?
7.answer: The input-validation process rejects 24.
table: Saved summary for the next session
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: The development life cycle
body: Analysis defines requirements using abstraction and decomposition.
Design uses structure diagrams, flowcharts and pseudocode.
Coding implements and tests components; testing checks the completed solution against requirements.
7.check: A correct-looking program fails when the input is 20. Which stage needs revisiting?
7.answer: Testing reveals the failure. Revisit the design or implementation, correct it and retest the requirement.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Decomposition and design methods
body: Main task: process a set of quiz scores.
Sub-tasks: read a valid score; calculate statistics; display results.
A structure diagram shows the hierarchy. A flowchart shows execution order and decisions.
7.check: Which sub-task could be reused for each of five scores?
7.answer: ReadValidScore can be called repeatedly instead of copying validation code.
7.teacher: Students draw a hierarchy and a flowchart for input validation. Use the linked official conventions PDF for terminal, process, input/output, decision and flow-line symbols.

7.title: A structure diagram shows the parts
body: The root names the complete system.
Each lower level breaks a task into smaller tasks.
Branches describe responsibility, not execution order.
7.check: Which branch handles switching the alarm on?
7.answer: Set alarm contains Turn alarm on/off.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: A flowchart shows the next step
body: Follow the arrows from START.
A decision selects a labelled branch.
Here, No waits and checks again. Yes sounds the alarm.
7.check: What happens when the current time does not match?
7.answer: Wait 30 seconds, get the time again, then repeat the comparison.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Decision symbols and assignments
body: The diamond contains a condition.
Yes and No must lead to the correct next instruction.
The rectangle changes the stored value.
7.check: Trace the diagram for X = 9 and B = 6.
7.answer: The comparison is true. B becomes 9.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Totalling, counting and averaging
body: Initialise the accumulator before the loop.
Count records by adding 1; total values by adding the value.
Divide only when the count is greater than zero.
7.check: For inputs 4, 7, 2, what is the final mean?
7.answer: Total = 13, Count = 3, Mean = 13 / 3. A count is not the total.
7.code:
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
    INPUT Score
    Total ← Total + Score
    Count ← Count + 1
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total / Count
7.teacher: Ask students to trace before revealing results.

7.title: A complete accumulator trace
body: Follow the algorithm exactly, including errors.
Record variable changes, prompts and output in execution order.
Do not silently repair code while tracing it.
7.check: What would change if Total were reset inside the loop?
7.answer: The final total would be 2 because earlier inputs would be discarded.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Maximum and minimum
body: Initialise Highest from the first item in a non-empty array.
Compare each remaining item with the current highest.
For a minimum, change the comparison to <.
7.check: Why is Highest ← 0 unsafe for arbitrary data?
7.answer: If all values are negative, zero is not in the list and is incorrectly reported as the maximum.
7.code:
Highest ← Scores[1]
FOR Index ← 2 TO 5
    IF Scores[Index] > Highest THEN
        Highest ← Scores[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Highest
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Maximum: a worked trace
body: Start with the first value, even when it is negative.
Replace Highest only when a larger value appears.
7.check: What comparison would find the minimum?
7.answer: Use Value < Lowest, with Lowest initially equal to the first value.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Linear search pseudocode
body: Compare the target with one element at a time.
Stop when a match is found or the list is exhausted.
This version records the first matching position, or 0 for not found.
7.check: For [4, 7, 2, 7, 9], searching for 7 returns what?
7.answer: Position 2, because the loop stops at the first match.
7.code:
Position ← 0
Index ← 1
WHILE Index <= 5 AND Position = 0 DO
    IF Scores[Index] = Target THEN
        Position ← Index
    ENDIF
    Index ← Index + 1
ENDWHILE
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Linear search: found and not found
body: Data: [4, 7, 2, 7, 9]. Indexing starts at 1.
The first matching index is the result.
If every comparison fails, Position remains 0.
7.check: How many comparisons locate 9?
7.answer: Five. A missing target also needs five comparisons in this list.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Swapping preserves both values
body: A temporary variable stores the value about to be overwritten.
Each assignment uses the values from the preceding row.
7.check: What goes wrong without Temp?
7.answer: After A becomes 2, copying A into B also gives 2. The original 7 is lost.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Bubble sort: the first pass
body: Compare adjacent values from left to right.
Swap only when the left value exceeds the right value.
7.check: Is the list fully sorted at the end of this pass?
7.answer: No. The largest value is in place, but 4, 2 and 1 still need sorting.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Bubble sort: later passes
body: Each pass moves another large value towards the right.
The simple version stops after a complete pass makes no swaps.
7.check: Why does this version execute pass 4?
7.answer: It confirms that there are no swaps. The loop stops using Swapped, not by looking at the list.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Bubble sort pseudocode
body: Compare neighbours and swap if they are in the wrong order.
After one ascending pass, the largest value is at the right end.
Repeat until a full pass makes no swaps.
7.check: One pass over [4, 7, 2, 1] produces which list?
7.answer: [4, 2, 1, 7]. One pass does not necessarily sort the entire list.
7.code:
REPEAT
    Swapped ← FALSE
    FOR Index ← 1 TO N - 1
        IF A[Index] > A[Index + 1] THEN
            Temp ← A[Index]
            A[Index] ← A[Index + 1]
            A[Index + 1] ← Temp
            Swapped ← TRUE
        ENDIF
    NEXT Index
UNTIL Swapped = FALSE
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Validation checks
body: A value can pass validation and still be factually wrong.
Combine checks where necessary: presence, type and range serve different purposes.
7.check: A student types 12 instead of 13; both are valid ages. Will a range check detect it?
7.answer: No. A range check tests acceptability, not whether the value matches the source.
table: Recalculate an appended digit to detect some entry errors
7.teacher: A check digit cannot guarantee error-free entry; discuss its limits.

7.title: Choosing a suitable validation check
body: Choose a rule that matches the requirement.
A value may satisfy one check and fail another.
7.check: Which checks suit a required six-character code?
7.answer: Presence and length. Add a format check if letters and digits must follow a specific pattern.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Check digits detect some entry errors
body: A rule calculates an extra digit from the other digits.
The program recalculates it when the identifier is entered.
A match does not guarantee that the identifier is correct.
7.check: Can a check digit prove that the product is the one intended?
7.answer: No. A different valid identifier may still pass the rule.
7.teacher: This simple sum rule is an original teaching example. It is not the ISBN or payment-card algorithm.

7.title: Verification checks
body: Visual check: compare entered data with the original source.
Double entry: enter data twice and compare the entries.
Neither method proves the original source is correct.
7.check: Two identical incorrect entries pass double entry. Why?
7.answer: The entries agree with each other. Agreement does not establish that either matches the intended value.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary data
body: For an integer score from 0 to 20 inclusive, test both accepted limits and adjacent rejected values.
A test plan needs input, expected result, actual result and a judgement.
7.check: Are extreme and boundary data identical?
7.answer: Extreme data are the accepted limits. Boundary data also include the neighbouring rejected values.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: A test plan makes expectations explicit
body: The accepted integer interval is 0 to 20 inclusive.
Choose expected results before running the program.
7.check: If 20 is rejected, which part of the condition may be wrong?
7.answer: A strict < 20 may have replaced <= 20.
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

7.title: Correcting a faulty condition
body: Requirement: reject any integer outside 0 to 20.
The condition below rejects no number.
Correct the Boolean logic and test all four boundary values.
7.check: Replace the faulty condition with a correct condition.
7.answer: Use Score < 0 OR Score > 20. A number cannot be below 0 AND above 20 simultaneously.
7.code:
IF Score < 0 AND Score > 20 THEN
    OUTPUT "Invalid"
ENDIF
7.teacher: Exit task: write a complete five-score algorithm with validation, total, highest and mean. Compare against the downloadable teacher solution. Homework: Hodder chapter 7 workbook, then PMT 7 questions.

7.title: Independent task: five valid scores
body: Read five integer scores, each from 0 to 20.
Reject invalid values without counting them.
Output the total, mean and highest score.
7.check: For inputs 4, 21, 7, 2, 1, 6, what should the outputs be?
7.answer: Reject 21. The five valid scores total 20, the mean is 4 and the maximum is 7.
7.teacher: Allow 8–10 minutes. Ask students to annotate their validation loop and accumulator initialisation. Use the next slide to discuss a possible solution.

7.title: Five scores: model algorithm
body: Zero is a safe initial maximum for scores from 0 to 20.
Only a valid score leaves the inner loop.
7.check: Why does an invalid entry not increase Index?
7.answer: REPEAT continues inside the current FOR iteration until the value is valid.
7.code:
Total ← 0
Highest ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
    REPEAT
        INPUT Score
    UNTIL Score >= 0 AND Score <= 20
    Total ← Total + Score
    IF Score > Highest THEN
        Highest ← Score
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total, Total / 5, Highest
7.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Variables, constants and data types
body: A variable can change; a constant retains its value.
Use meaningful identifiers and declare types explicitly in pseudocode.
8.check: What type suits a score average? What type suits a phone number?
8.answer: Average: REAL. Phone number: STRING, because leading zeros matter and arithmetic is inappropriate.
8.teacher: Classroom Python is provided separately; most exam coding responses must use pseudocode.

8.title: Declarations and meaningful names
body: A declaration states the identifier and its data type.
A named constant makes a fixed rule easy to find.
8.check: Why is MaxScore clearer than M?
8.answer: Its name describes the value’s purpose without requiring the reader to guess.
8.code:
CONSTANT MaxScore = 20
DECLARE Score, Count : INTEGER
DECLARE Mean : REAL
DECLARE StudentName : STRING
DECLARE Grade : CHAR
DECLARE Valid : BOOLEAN
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Sequence, input and output
body: Instructions execute in order unless a control structure changes the flow.
Assignment stores a value; OUTPUT displays it.
8.check: What does the final OUTPUT show if Price = 8.5 and Quantity = 3?
8.answer: 25.5. Changing the order to calculate before input would use undefined or old values.
8.code:
DECLARE Price, Cost : REAL
DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
INPUT Price
INPUT Quantity
Cost ← Price * Quantity
OUTPUT "Cost: ", Cost
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Assignment changes the current value
body: Evaluate the right side using the current values.
Then replace the value stored on the left.
8.check: What does OUTPUT X display?
8.answer: 6. Y remains 5 because it stored the earlier value of X + 3.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: IF selects a branch
body: The condition produces TRUE or FALSE.
Only the selected branch runs.
8.check: Which output appears for Mark = 50?
8.answer: Pass, because 50 >= 50 is TRUE.
8.code:
IF Mark >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Pass"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Try again"
ENDIF
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: CASE selects a matching value
body: IF can test a Boolean expression or a range.
CASE is useful when one value selects among discrete choices.
The optional OTHERWISE branch handles unmatched values.
8.check: What is output for Choice = 3?
8.answer: Invalid choice. Only 1 and 2 have matching branches.
8.code:
CASE OF Choice
    1 : OUTPUT "Add"
    2 : OUTPUT "Search"
    OTHERWISE OUTPUT "Invalid choice"
ENDCASE
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Nested selection
body: An inner IF runs only when its outer branch runs.
Indentation shows which ENDIF closes each IF.
8.check: What happens when Member = FALSE and Age = 12?
8.answer: The outer ELSE outputs Standard. The inner age comparison does not run.
8.code:
IF Member = TRUE THEN
    IF Age < 16 THEN
        OUTPUT "Junior member"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Adult member"
    ENDIF
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Standard"
ENDIF
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Choosing a loop
body: FOR suits a known number of repetitions.
WHILE tests before the body and may run zero times.
REPEAT tests after the body and runs at least once.
8.check: Which loop naturally fits prompting until input is valid?
8.answer: REPEAT…UNTIL. Input must be requested at least once; stop when the valid condition is TRUE.
table: Continue while the condition is TRUE
Stop when the condition becomes TRUE
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: FOR loops: the counter and total
body: The counter changes automatically at NEXT.
Initialise Total before entering the loop.
8.check: What is Total after the third iteration?
8.answer: 6, because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
8.code:
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
    Total ← Total + Index
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Pre-condition and post-condition loops
body: WHILE tests before the body.
REPEAT tests after the body.
The same starting value can lead to a different number of executions.
8.check: If X starts at 5, how many times does each body run?
8.answer: WHILE runs zero times. REPEAT runs once and leaves X equal to 6.
8.code:
X ← 5
WHILE X < 3 DO
    X ← X + 1
ENDWHILE

X ← 5
REPEAT
    X ← X + 1
UNTIL X >= 3
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: A validation loop
body: The stopping condition describes valid input.
Both lower and upper limits must be satisfied.
This example assumes the input is already an integer.
8.check: Why use AND in UNTIL but OR in a rejection condition?
8.answer: A valid value must meet both limits. An invalid value only needs to violate one limit.
8.code:
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Enter score, 0 to 20"
    INPUT Score
UNTIL Score >= 0 AND Score <= 20
8.teacher: Type checking is a separate requirement. In classroom Python, catch a conversion error before checking the numeric range.

8.title: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators
body: Arithmetic calculates; relational operators compare; logical operators combine conditions.
In pseudocode, = compares and ← assigns.
Use parentheses to make a compound condition explicit.
8.check: Evaluate 17 DIV 5 and 17 MOD 5.
8.teacher: Ask students to contrast Python assignment = and comparison == with pseudocode notation.

8.title: DIV and MOD divide a quantity differently
body: 17 objects can fill three groups of five.
DIV gives the whole-number quotient. MOD gives the remainder.
8.check: What are 23 DIV 4 and 23 MOD 4?
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: String functions
body: Declare the indexing convention before taking a substring.
Cambridge examples generally use position 1 for the first character.
A substring uses a start position and a length, not an end position.
8.check: With Code = "Cambridge", what is SUBSTRING(Code, 4, 3)?
8.answer: "bri". Positions 4, 5 and 6 are selected.
8.code:
Code ← "Cambridge"
OUTPUT LENGTH(Code)       // 9
OUTPUT UCASE(Code)        // CAMBRIDGE
OUTPUT LCASE(Code)        // cambridge
OUTPUT SUBSTRING(Code, 1, 3) // Cam
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Substring positions
body: This example uses position 1 for the first character.
The third argument of SUBSTRING gives a length.
8.check: What is SUBSTRING("Cambridge", 4, 3)?
8.answer: bri, using positions 4, 5 and 6.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Procedures perform a task
body: Parameters supply values to a reusable task.
CALL runs the procedure.
8.check: What output follows this call?
8.answer: Hello Ada.
8.code:
PROCEDURE Greet(Name : STRING)
    OUTPUT "Hello ", Name
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL Greet("Ada")
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Functions return a value
body: A procedure is called to carry out a task.
A function returns a value that can be used in an expression.
Parameters carry values into the subprogram.
8.check: Which item is the parameter, and which values are arguments?
8.answer: X is the parameter in the definition. Scores[1] and 10 are arguments in the calls.
8.code:
FUNCTION Double(X : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
    RETURN X * 2
ENDFUNCTION
OUTPUT Double(Scores[1])
OUTPUT Double(10)
8.teacher: Add a procedure example orally: PROCEDURE ShowScore(Value : INTEGER), OUTPUT Value, ENDPROCEDURE; invoke with CALL ShowScore(10).

8.title: A function call: arguments and return value
body: Arguments fill the parameters for one call.
RETURN sends one result back to the calling expression.
8.check: What value does MeanOfTwo(8, 12) return?
8.answer: 10. The returned value can be assigned, displayed or used in another calculation.
8.code:
FUNCTION MeanOfTwo(A : REAL, B : REAL)
    RETURNS REAL
    RETURN (A + B) / 2
ENDFUNCTION

Result ← MeanOfTwo(8, 12)
OUTPUT Result
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Local and global scope
body: A local variable is accessible within its subprogram.
A global variable can be accessed across the program in its declared scope.
Prefer parameters and return values when they make dependencies clearer.
8.check: Why is changing an unrelated global Total inside a function risky?
8.answer: Other parts of the program may depend on Total. The side effect makes behaviour harder to trace and reuse.
8.teacher: Maintenance checklist: meaningful names; short subprograms; comments explaining non-obvious purpose; consistent indentation. Avoid comments that merely repeat every line.

8.title: ROUND and RANDOM
body: Version 6 permits ROUND on an identifier or an expression.
RANDOM() returns a value from 0 to 1 inclusive in Cambridge pseudocode.
Different programming languages have different random-number APIs.
8.check: Does ROUND(RANDOM() * 6, 0) model a fair six-sided die?
8.answer: No. It can return 0 and the rounding intervals are not equally wide. In classroom Python, use randint(1, 6) for a die.
8.code:
Mean ← ROUND(Total / Count, 2)
R ← RANDOM()
Remainder ← 17 MOD 5
Quotient ← 17 DIV 5
8.teacher: Source: 2026–2028 syllabus Version 6, page 41. Count must be positive before the division. The die is a reasoning extension, not an extra required library routine.

8.title: Maintainable programs
body: Names describe the data or task.
Comments explain a rule or reason.
A subprogram keeps one reusable task in one place.
8.check: Which comment explains the reason for the calculation?
8.answer: “Convert minutes to hours for the report” explains purpose more clearly than “divide by 60”.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: One-dimensional arrays
body: One index identifies one element.
This textbook example uses indexes 0 to 9.
The ten elements have the same data type.
8.check: What value is stored at index 1 in the diagram?
8.answer: 19. Index 1 is the second element in this zero-based array.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Declaring and traversing an array
body: One identifier names a collection of elements with one data type.
An index selects an element. Keep every index within the declared bounds.
8.check: Which index is invalid for Scores: 0, 1 or 5?
8.answer: 0 is invalid for the declared 1…5 bounds. Zero-based arrays are also allowed if used consistently.
8.code:
DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
    INPUT Scores[Index]
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Scores[3]
8.teacher: Use a row of five labelled boxes on the classroom board and trace reads and writes.

8.title: Array bounds and element count
body: The declaration determines every legal index.
For inclusive bounds, count = upper − lower + 1.
8.check: How many elements does ARRAY[0:4] contain?
8.answer: Five, at indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Two-dimensional arrays
body: The first index selects a row. The second selects a column.
This textbook diagram uses row and column indexes starting at 0.
8.check: What is MyTable[1, 2] in the diagram?
8.answer: 48, in the second row and third column.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Nested iteration through a 2D array
body: Rows identify students; columns identify quiz attempts.
Use nested iteration to visit every cell.
Reset a row total inside the outer loop, before the inner loop.
8.check: How many additions are performed for 3 students and 2 quizzes?
8.answer: Six additions. Each of the three row totals receives two values.
8.code:
DECLARE Mark : ARRAY[1:3, 1:2] OF INTEGER
// Assume Mark has already been populated
FOR Student ← 1 TO 3
    Total ← 0
    FOR Quiz ← 1 TO 2
        Total ← Total + Mark[Student, Quiz]
    NEXT Quiz
    OUTPUT Total
NEXT Student
8.teacher: Assume all array values have been populated before this fragment. Ask what happens if Total is initialised only once before both loops.

8.title: A row-total trace
body: Mark contains rows [4, 7], [2, 20], [0, 6].
Reset Total when a new student starts.
8.check: What would happen if Total were initialised only once?
8.answer: The outputs would be cumulative: 11, 33 and 39 instead of 11, 22 and 6.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Writing persistent data
body: Open the file in WRITE mode before writing.
Close it when the operation finishes.
WRITE can replace existing contents.
8.check: What should the file contain after this code?
8.answer: A line containing Ada,20. Reopen the file in READ mode to check it.
8.code:
OPENFILE "summary.txt" FOR WRITE
Line ← "Ada,20"
WRITEFILE "summary.txt", Line
CLOSEFILE "summary.txt"
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Reading a file until the end
body: Variables normally disappear when a program finishes; files preserve data.
Open a file in the intended mode, read or write, then close it.
Writing to a file may replace its previous contents.
8.check: What must be checked before reading repeatedly to the end of a file?
8.answer: Use an end-of-file check so the program does not attempt to read past the final line.
8.code:
OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("scores.txt") DO
    READFILE "scores.txt", Line
    OUTPUT Line
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"
8.teacher: Writing counterpart: OPENFILE "result.txt" FOR WRITE; WRITEFILE "result.txt", Line; CLOSEFILE "result.txt". Student task: read a name, save it, reopen and display it.

8.title: The file cursor and EOF
body: Suppose the file has two lines: Ada,20 and Ben,15.
Check for end of file before reading another line.
8.check: Why should the program check EOF before READFILE?
8.answer: There may be no next line to read, including when the file is empty.
8.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

8.title: Complete programming task
body: Read five validated scores into an array.
Calculate total, mean and highest using named subprograms.
Save a summary; then reopen it to confirm the result.
8.check: Which tests cover both validation and calculation?
8.answer: Try all zeros, all twenties, mixed scores, a rejected −1 and 21, and invalid text. Verify expected totals, means, highest values and saved output.
8.teacher: Suggested lesson 4: practical project. Start with the student brief and use the supplied Python model only after planning. For the exam 15-mark scenario, pseudocode, Python, Visual Basic or Java are allowed; use pseudocode for other coding questions.

9.title: Fields, records and tables
body: A row stores one record.
A column holds one field across all records.
A table describes one type of entity.
9.check: In a BOOK table, is Price a field or a record?
9.answer: A field. A complete row describes one book.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: The BOOK table
body: A record describes one item; a field describes one attribute.
A table stores records with the same field structure.
Decide what must be stored before choosing field names and types.
9.check: In BOOK, is Price a record or a field?
9.answer: Price is a field. The complete row for B01 is a record.
9.teacher: Use this same BOOK data throughout the lesson and downloadable SQL practical.

9.title: Choosing database field types
body: Store a telephone number as text to preserve leading zeros.
Use a date/time type for dates; a Boolean for a two-state value.
Validation checks whether entered data meets rules.
9.answer: A numeric type check and a range check such as Price >= 0. A valid number can still be the wrong price.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Six database data types
body: Choose the type from the meaning of the value.
Numbers used as identifiers may belong in text fields.
9.check: Why can a telephone number be text?
9.answer: Leading zeros and symbols matter, and arithmetic has no useful meaning for the identifier.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Primary keys
body: Every record needs a unique key value.
Choose a stable identifier rather than a name that may repeat.
A key must not be missing.
9.check: Why is Title a poor primary key?
9.answer: Different books or editions can share a title. BookID can be assigned a unique value to each record.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Primary-key suitability
body: Every record needs a unique, non-empty key.
Names and prices can repeat.
9.check: Can a changing stock quantity be a suitable key?
9.answer: No. Quantities can repeat and change. A dedicated BookID is a better choice.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Validation in a database
body: A field type limits the kind of value stored.
Additional rules check whether the value is acceptable.
9.check: Does Price >= 0 prove the price matches the source?
9.answer: No. It only rejects negative prices.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: SELECT, FROM and WHERE
body: FROM names the single source table.
WHERE tests each record against a condition.
Text values need quotation marks.
9.answer: Algorithms 12; Logic 9; Databases 15. The displayed row order is not guaranteed without ORDER BY.
9.teacher: Students predict the result on paper before running the supplied SQLite exercise.

9.title: SELECT and WHERE: the result
body: WHERE keeps B01, B03 and B04 because InStock is TRUE.
SELECT displays only Title and Price.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: A condition applies to each record
body: For Price >= 12, compare each record’s Price with 12.
A true comparison includes that record.
9.check: Does the query include a book priced exactly 12?
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Filtering and sorting
body: ORDER BY specifies the sorting field and direction.
The field used for sorting need not be displayed.
Cambridge uses ASCENDING / DESCENDING; SQLite uses ASC / DESC.
9.answer: Databases (15), then Algorithms (12). Programming is excluded because InStock is FALSE.
9.code:
SELECT Title, Price
FROM BOOK
WHERE InStock = TRUE AND Price >= 10
ORDER BY Price DESCENDING;
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: ORDER BY: the result
body: First retain in-stock books priced at least 10.
Then order Price from high to low.
9.check: What changes if the direction is ASCENDING?
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: AND, OR and parentheses
body: AND requires both conditions. OR requires at least one.
Parentheses make the intended grouping clear.
Read the Boolean condition for each record before selecting it.
9.answer: B03 and B04. B02 meets Price > 14 but fails the stock condition.
9.code:
SELECT BookID
FROM BOOK
WHERE InStock = TRUE
AND (Price < 10 OR Price > 14);
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: A compound-condition trace
body: Condition: InStock AND (Price < 10 OR Price > 14).
The parentheses keep the price alternatives together.
9.check: Which BookIDs satisfy the entire condition?
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: COUNT and SUM
body: COUNT(*) counts matching records.
SUM(Price) adds the numeric Price values of matching records.
An aggregate query produces a summary result.
9.check: What are the two results for the BOOK data?
9.answer: COUNT(*) = 3; SUM(Price) = 36. COUNT(Price) counts non-null Price values rather than adding them.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Aggregate results
body: The matching in-stock prices are 12, 9 and 15.
COUNT(*) counts rows. SUM(Price) adds their prices.
9.check: Would COUNT(*) change if Algorithms cost 14?
9.answer: No. There would still be three matching records. SUM would increase to 38.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Independent SQL task
body: Request: show titles of in-stock books below 16, cheapest first.
Identify displayed fields, source table, filter and sort separately.
Predict the output before running the query.
9.check: Write the query and ordered result.
9.answer: SELECT Title FROM BOOK WHERE InStock = TRUE AND Price < 16 ORDER BY Price ASCENDING; Result: Logic, Algorithms, Databases.
9.teacher: Exit task: design a single-table equipment-loan database with a suitable primary key, six field types across examples, validation and two queries. Homework: Hodder chapter 9 workbook and PMT 9. No JOIN is required for this syllabus.

9.title: SQL task: model answer
body: Only in-stock books below 16 qualify.
Show the Title field and sort by Price from low to high.
9.check: List the output titles in their final order.
9.code:
SELECT Title
FROM BOOK
WHERE InStock = TRUE AND Price < 16
ORDER BY Price ASCENDING;
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

9.title: Common SQL errors
body: Check displayed fields, source table, filter and order separately.
Cambridge exam syntax uses ASCENDING and DESCENDING.
9.check: Which clause specifies the table name?
9.answer: FROM. A query result does not itself change the stored records.
9.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Boolean values and logic gates
body: Use 0 / 1 or FALSE / TRUE consistently.
A gate maps input values to one output.
NOT has one input; the other required gates have two inputs.
10.check: How many input combinations are possible for three independent inputs?
10.teacher: Open the existing practice page for the six standard gate-symbol diagrams and compare with syllabus page 33.

10.title: NOT gate
body: The output reverses the input.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: If A = 0, what is X?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: AND gate
body: Both inputs must be 1.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: What is X for A = 1 and B = 0?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: OR gate
body: At least one input must be 1.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: Does OR include the case where both inputs are 1?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: XOR gate
body: Exactly one input must be 1.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: How do OR and XOR differ for 11?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: NAND gate
body: Invert the output of AND.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: Which input pair gives a NAND output of 0?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: NOR gate
body: Invert the output of OR.
Read inputs on the left and the output on the right.
10.check: Which input pair gives a NOR output of 1?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Comparing the five two-input gates
body: AND: both 1. OR: at least one 1. XOR: exactly one 1.
NAND is NOT AND; NOR is NOT OR.
NOT reverses its single input: 0 → 1 and 1 → 0.
10.check: Which gates give 1 when both inputs are 1?
10.answer: AND and OR. NAND, NOR and XOR give 0 for 11.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Truth-table input combinations
body: For n independent inputs, list 2^n combinations.
Three inputs require eight rows, from 000 to 111.
10.check: What changes fastest in this ordering?
10.answer: C changes every row. B changes every two rows. A changes every four rows.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: An alarm problem statement
body: A = door sensor active; B = window sensor active; C = alarm disabled.
The alarm sounds if either sensor is active AND the alarm is not disabled.
Write the expression before drawing the circuit.
10.check: Write the alarm expression using A, B and C.
10.answer: X = (A OR B) AND NOT C. OR is inclusive: both sensors may be active.
10.code:
P = A OR B
Q = NOT C
X = P AND Q
10.teacher: For a circuit, connect A and B to OR; connect C to NOT; connect the two intermediate outputs to AND. Do not simplify away gates specified by the statement.

10.title: Alarm: intermediate values
body: A = door active. B = window active. C = alarm disabled.
P = A OR B. Q = NOT C. X = P AND Q.
10.check: For A = 1, B = 0, C = 1, find P, Q and X.
10.answer: P = 1, Q = 0, X = 0. Disabling the alarm prevents the sensor from sounding it.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Alarm: the complete truth table
body: List all eight inputs in binary counting order.
Compute P and Q before computing X.
A complete truth table includes every combination once.
10.check: Why is X = 0 for A = 1, B = 1, C = 1?
10.answer: The alarm is disabled: Q = NOT C = 0. Therefore P AND Q = 0.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: An expression from output-1 rows
body: For each output-1 row, create an AND term matching its input values.
Use NOT for a 0 input and the unchanged variable for a 1 input.
Join those row terms with OR.
10.check: For two inputs, only 01 and 10 give output 1. Write an expression.
10.answer: (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B). This has XOR behaviour; follow the requested form when drawing a circuit.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Truth table to expression: a worked example
body: The only output-1 rows are 01 and 10.
Write one AND term for each selected row, then join with OR.
10.check: Write an expression without using XOR.
10.answer: (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: An expression becomes a circuit
body: This branch represents (NOT S AND T).
S passes through NOT before entering AND.
T enters the other AND input directly.
10.check: For S = 0 and T = 1, what is the branch output?
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Combining two branches
body: The upper branch is NOT S AND T.
The lower branch is S AND W.
OR combines their two outputs.
10.check: Write the expression shown by this circuit.
10.answer: (NOT S AND T) OR (S AND W).
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: A circuit with three inputs
body: A third branch adds (NOT T AND W).
Two-input OR gates join the three branch results.
The circuit retains every branch in the given expression.
10.check: How many NOT, AND and OR gates appear?
10.answer: Two NOT gates, three AND gates and two OR gates.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Circuit trace: named intermediate values
body: P = NOT S AND T. Q = S AND W. R = NOT T AND W.
Final output X = (P OR Q) OR R.
10.check: For S = 0, T = 1, W = 0, which branch makes X equal 1?
10.answer: P = 1. Q and R are both 0.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Constructing a circuit from an expression
body: Use at most two inputs per non-NOT gate.
Build longer expressions from a sequence of two-input gates.
For 2026–2028, draw the statement as given without simplification.
10.check: How do you build (A AND B) OR (NOT A AND C)?
10.answer: Create the two AND results separately, including NOT A, then feed their outputs into an OR gate.
10.code:
P = A AND B
Q = NOT A
R = Q AND C
X = P OR R
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Independent circuit task
body: Name every intermediate output.
Trace one test input through all gates.
Then complete the truth table and compare it with the problem statement.
10.check: For (A AND B) OR (NOT A AND C), find X when A = 0, B = 1, C = 1.
10.answer: P = 0, Q = 1, R = 1, X = 1. The unselected branch cannot change this OR result.
10.teacher: Exit task: draw the circuit, enumerate all eight rows, then explain in words when X is 1. Homework: Hodder chapter 10 workbook then PMT 10. Full adders in the textbook are enrichment, not an extra 2026–2028 requirement.

10.title: Circuit task: model truth table
body: P = A AND B. Q = NOT A. R = Q AND C.
X = P OR R. All eight combinations appear once.
10.check: Describe how A controls the result.
10.answer: When A = 1, X follows B. When A = 0, X follows C. Keep the original gates when the question asks for the unsimplified circuit.
10.teacher: Ask students to predict first, explain their reasoning, then compare with the model answer. Use the linked chapter workbook for independent practice.

10.title: Logic-circuit checks
body: Use one input for NOT and two for each other required gate.
Label external inputs, intermediate results and the final output.
Keep all branches required by the original statement.
10.check: What does a small circle on a gate’s output mean?
10.answer: Inversion. It changes each 0 to 1 and each 1 to 0.
10.teacher: Check one complete input trace before completing the whole truth table. Use the chapter workbook and PMT Topic 10 questions for further practice.
